questions.question: What should you do if the Hazardous Materials Table shows "Forbidden" in the third column?

options.text: Transport the substance by air only.
Transport the substance only at night.
Transport the substance with a security guard.

questions.explanation: The third column of the Hazardous Materials Table shows the hazard class. Never transport any material marked "Forbidden."

questions.question: How many identical placards must be placed on a vehicle carrying hazardous materials?
questions.explanation: Placards must be placed on all four sides of the vehicle.

questions.question: How should hazardous materials be shown on a shipping paper that also lists non-hazardous materials?

options.text: List them at the bottom of the paper.
List them at the top of the paper.
Highlight them in the same color as non-hazardous materials.

questions.correctAnswerText: List them at the top of the paper.
questions.explanation: Hazardous materials must be listed first, highlighted in a different color, or marked with an "X" in a column labeled "HM."

questions.question: Where should shipping papers be kept?

options.text: Easy to see when someone enters the cab.

questions.correctAnswerText: Easy to see when someone enters the cab.
questions.explanation: Keep shipping papers in a pouch on the driver's side door or in another easy-to-reach spot. They must be easy to see for anyone entering the cab.

questions.question: How must placards be positioned?

options.text: In any way, as long as they are visible.
So words and numbers can be read from left to right.
Within three inches of other markings.

questions.correctAnswerText: So words and numbers can be read from left to right.
questions.explanation: Placards must be positioned so words and numbers read from left to right. Keep them at least three inches away from other markings.

questions.question: How should you label a hazardous material package that is too small for the label?

options.text: Tie it with other hazardous materials and put a labeled sheet of paper on the outside.
Attach the label to a tag that is securely fastened to the package.
Mark it with a large orange dot.
Place it in a box with a warning label.

questions.correctAnswerText: Attach the label to a tag that is securely fastened to the package.
questions.explanation: If the diamond-shaped label does not fit on the package, attach it to a tag that is securely fastened to the package.

questions.question: Who must identify the hazard class of materials being shipped?
questions.explanation: The shipper is responsible for identifying the product number, shipping name, hazard class, packing group, and correct packaging, labels, marking, and placards.

questions.question: What is the correct way to check tire pressure?

options.text: Push on the tires to feel the pressure.

questions.explanation: Check each tire at the start of your trip. A tire pressure gauge is the only accurate way to check tire pressure.

questions.question: What should you do if you suspect a leak in radioactive material?

options.text: Go to the local fire department.
Pick up any loose pieces of the material.
Continue carrying the cargo, just avoid touching the leak.
Do not drive the vehicle until it is cleaned.

questions.correctAnswerText: Do not drive the vehicle until it is cleaned.
questions.explanation: If you suspect a leak in radioactive material, tell your dispatcher immediately. Do not touch the material. Do not drive the vehicle until it has been cleaned or checked with a survey meter.

questions.question: What must you do at a railroad crossing when carrying chlorine?

options.text: Slow down before crossing the tracks.
Proceed if no warning lights are flashing.
Proceed if no other vehicles are in sight.

questions.explanation: When transporting any amount of chlorine, you must always stop 15 to 50 feet from the nearest track at a railroad crossing.

questions.question: Who can transport hazardous materials?

options.text: Any driver, as long as the hazardous materials weigh less than 50 pounds.
Any driver in a rural area.
A driver with a CDL and a HazMat endorsement.

questions.correctAnswerText: A driver with a CDL and a HazMat endorsement.
questions.explanation: You need a CDL with a hazardous materials endorsement to drive any vehicle that transports hazardous materials.

questions.question: Where can you find identification numbers for chemicals?

options.text: In the DOT Emergency Response Guidebook.

questions.correctAnswerText: In the DOT Emergency Response Guidebook.
questions.explanation: The DOT Emergency Response Guidebook lists all hazardous chemicals and their identification numbers.

questions.question: What do you need to know to choose the right placards?

options.text: The hazard class of the materials.
The type of containers holding the materials.

questions.correctAnswerText: The hazard class of the materials.
questions.explanation: You must know the hazard class of the materials, the amount being shipped, and the total weight of all hazardous materials in the vehicle to choose the right placards.

questions.question: If the letter "G" appears in Column 1 of a shipping paper, what else must be listed?

options.text: The technical name of the hazardous material.
The type of packaging containing the hazardous material.
The date the product was packed.

questions.correctAnswerText: The technical name of the hazardous material.
questions.explanation: If the letter "G" (for "Generic") appears in Column 1 of a shipping paper, the technical name of the hazardous material must also be listed.

questions.question: Who is responsible for putting placards on a vehicle?
questions.explanation: The shipper provides the placards, but the driver is responsible for placing them on the vehicle.

questions.question: Where should a hazardous material's identification number appear?

options.text: On a bumper sticker on the vehicle.

questions.explanation: The ID number must appear on the shipping paper, the packaging, cargo tanks, and other bulk packaging.

questions.question: What should you do before opening trailer doors during a truck fire?

options.text: Check to see if the doors are hot.

questions.correctAnswerText: Check to see if the doors are hot.
questions.explanation: Feel the doors to check if they are hot before opening them. If the doors are hot, there may be a cargo fire. Keep the doors closed if there is a cargo fire.

questions.question: How should hazardous materials be loaded and unloaded?
questions.explanation: Many hazardous materials become more dangerous when exposed to heat. Always load and unload them away from heat sources.

questions.question: What letters appear on shipping papers and packages for substances in reportable quantities?
questions.explanation: The letters "RQ" must appear on the shipping paper and package to indicate a reportable quantity.

questions.question: What is important to know about radioactive materials packages?

options.text: Radiation will pass through to other packages.
The package should be placed in the cab.
The package should be loaded on its side.
The package should be made of wood.

questions.correctAnswerText: Radiation will pass through to other packages.
questions.explanation: Radiation passes through each radioactive materials package to all nearby packages. Rules control how many packages can be loaded together.

questions.question: For small packages that cannot hold a HazMat label, how should materials be labeled?
questions.explanation: If a package is too small for a label, attach the label to a tag secured to the package.

questions.question: What should a carrier do if hazardous materials are not properly prepared?

options.text: Accept the shipment and note it on the paperwork

questions.explanation: Carriers must refuse shipments of hazardous materials that are not properly prepared.

questions.question: After delivering compressed gas, you should turn off the engine ____ unhooking the hoses.
questions.explanation: Turn off the engine after product transfer but before unhooking the hoses.

questions.question: Many products classed as poison are also:
questions.explanation: Many poisonous products are also flammable. Take proper precautions if your cargo may be flammable.

questions.question: Which level of government controls hazardous materials laws?
questions.explanation: Federal, state, and local governments all make regulations for transporting hazardous materials.

questions.question: Before loading or unloading flammable liquids, the engine should be:
questions.explanation: Turn off the engine before loading or unloading flammable liquids, unless you need the engine to run a pump.

questions.question: If cargo is leaking, what should you do?

options.text: Touch the leaking material to identify it.
Use shipping papers and labels to identify the cargo.

questions.correctAnswerText: Use shipping papers and labels to identify the cargo.
questions.explanation: Identify leaking hazardous materials using shipping papers and labels. Do not touch the leaking material.

questions.question: How many hazardous materials classes exist?
questions.explanation: There are nine hazardous materials classes. Each class shows the risks of that type of material.

questions.question: How long must shippers keep copies of shipping papers?
questions.explanation: Shippers must keep copies of hazardous materials shipping papers for at least two years after the carrier accepts them.

questions.question: How should containers of nitric acid be stacked?

options.text: No more than two containers high
Loaded on top of other products

questions.correctAnswerText: No more than two containers high
questions.explanation: Nitric acid containers may be stacked, but only up to two containers high. Never stack them on top of other products.
